questions.q: Why does the lesson say a backup plan that only exists in one person's head is 'exactly as fragile' as the untested maintenance plan from Lesson 1?
options: Because it depends entirely on that one person being available and remembering correctly, which is the same unverified-trust problem as a never-tested maintenance plan
Because mental plans are technically impossible to execute in an emergency
Because Azure requires all backup plans to be stored in writing by policy
Because a spoken plan cannot legally satisfy healthcare compliance requirements
questions.explain: Both failure modes share the same root problem: untested trust. A plan nobody has verified or written down is a hypothesis, whether that's a backup job or a person's memory.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in the runbook's 'Restore procedure' section, according to the lesson?
options: The exact Portal steps and CLI command from Lesson 7, with real resource group, server, and database names filled in
A general description like 'use the Azure Portal to restore the database when needed'
A link to Microsoft's generic restore documentation, with no project-specific details
Only the T-SQL RESTORE DATABASE syntax used for on-prem SQL Server
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that exact commands with real names filled in are usable during an incident — vague descriptions are not.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'Run the restore CLI command' as a runbook instruction is 'useless at 2am'?
options: Because it assumes knowledge a stressed, unfamiliar teammate wouldn't have — the actual command with real names filled in is what's usable
Because CLI commands cannot be run outside business hours
Because az sql db restore only works during Azure's maintenance window
Because restores are technically disabled overnight for safety
questions.explain: A description assumes context a reader under pressure may not have; the literal, filled-in command is what someone can actually execute without guessing.

questions.q: What does the lesson call the single most important line in the entire runbook?
options: The last tested restore — its date, how long it took, and what was verified
The name of the Azure subscription
The list of every table in the database
The price tier of the database
questions.explain: The 'last tested restore' entry is what proves the plan has actually been verified, not just assumed to work — directly answering Priya's original question from Lesson 1.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is writing the runbook, in relation to the rest of the capstone's work?
options: Not a formality after the real work — it IS the real work, made durable
An optional nice-to-have that can be skipped if the backups are already tested
A separate project unrelated to the backup strategy built in earlier lessons
Something only needed if the database stores non-healthcare data
questions.explain: The runbook is explicitly the deliverable Priya asked for in Lesson 1 — everything built in Lessons 2-8 exists to make this document true and specific rather than aspirational.
